claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based multianalyte profiling data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: PCA of Luminex profiles identified factors contributing to the differential nature of the secretome between TOs and DOs, which included the enrichment of factors including CXCL1, CXCL5, and IL-8 in DOs versus IL-6 and IL28A/IFN-λ2 in TOs.
claims.source: PCA of these Luminex profiles identified factors contributing to the differential nature of the secretome between TOs and DOs, which included the enrichment of factors including CXCL1, CXCL5, and IL-8 in DOs versus IL-6 and IL28A/IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis of Luminex data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: Human chorionic villous explants release numerous cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that impact both maternal and fetal antimicrobial defenses.
claims.source: We have shown previously that human chorionic villous explants release numerous cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors that impact both maternal and fetal antimicrobial defenses (Corry et al., 2017; Megli et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Corry et al., 2017 and Megli et al., 2021.

claims.claim: PHTs isolated from mid-gestation and full-term placentas secrete immunomodulatory factors.
claims.source: Similarly, we have shown that PHTs isolated from mid-gestation and full-term placentas secrete some of these same immunomodulatory factors (Corry et al., 2017; Megli et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Corry et al., 2017 and Megli et al., 2021.

claims.claim: TOs recapitulated the phenotype of constitutive release of type III IFNs and released high levels of IFN-λ2, but not type I IFNs or IFN-λ1.
claims.source: We found that TOs recapitulated this phenotype and released high levels of IFN-λ2, but not type I IFNs or IFN-λ1 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: DOs did not basally secrete any detectable IFNs.
claims.source: In contrast, DOs did not basally secrete any detectable IFNs (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The levels of released IFN-λ2 from TOs were comparable to those from PHT cells and from matched cultured villous explants.
claims.source: The levels of released IFN-λ2 were comparable to those from PHT cells and from matched cultured villous explants (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparative Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The release of IFN-λ2 from TOs was detectable by ~10 days post-plating and reached high levels by >14 days in culture.
claims.source: We monitored the release of IFN-λ2 over the growth period of TOs and found that its release was detectable by ~10 days post-plating and reached high levels by >14 days in culture, which correlated with similar trends for IL-6 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by longitudinal Luminex assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CM isolated from TOs, but not DOs, induced interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) in cells treated with this CM using a HEK293-based reporter assay.
claims.source: We confirmed that CM isolated from TOs, but not DOs, induced interferon-s (ISGs) in cells treated with this CM using a HEK293-based reporter assay (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells.
claims.source: Consistent with this, CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells (Figure 4E) and in DOs (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TO-derived CM exerts potent antiviral effects on non-placental cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ZIKV infection assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: CM isolated from TOs reduced ZIKV infection in DOs.
claims.source: Consistent with this, CM isolated from TOs was antiviral and reduced ZIKV infection in CM-treated non-placental cells including U2OS cells (Figure 4E) and in DOs (Figure 4F and G), confirming that TO-derived CM exerts potent antiviral effects on non-placental cells.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by ZIKV infection assay data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claims.claim: TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2.
claims.source: Finally, we found that TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2, suggesting that EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs.
claims.source: Finally, we found that TOs differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype exhibited significantly reduced levels of secreted IFN-λ2, suggesting that EVTs are not the primary producers of IFN-λ2 in TOs (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EVT-differentiated TOs have reduced IFN-λ2 secretion.

claims.claim: Both TOs and DOs robustly responded to poly I:C treatment, which corresponded with significant transcriptional changes as assessed by RNASeq.
claims.source: We found that both TOs and DOs robustly responded to poly I:C treatment, which corresponded with significant transcriptional changes as assessed by RNASeq (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: TOs upregulated 448 transcripts in response to poly I:C treatment whereas DOs upregulated 121.
claims.source: Comparison of the transcripts induced by poly I:C treatment (as defined by significance of p<0.01 and log2 fold-change of ±2) of TOs and DOs revealed that TOs upregulated 448 transcripts whereas DOs upregulated 121 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Only 69 transcripts were shared between TOs and DOs in response to poly I:C treatment, the majority of which (64 of 69) were ISGs.
claims.source: Of these, only 69 were shared between TOs and DOs, the majority of which (64 of 69) were ISGs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram and heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: TOs induced the expression of chemokines including CXCL5 (log2 fold change 5.9), CX3CL1 (log2 fold change 7.1), and CCL22 (log2 fold change 7.6) in response to poly I:C treatment, which were the most induced cytokine or chemokine transcripts in poly I:C-treated TOs.
claims.source: Of the differentially induced transcripts, TOs induced the expression of chemokines including CXCL5 (log2 fold change 5.9), CX3CL1 (log2 fold change 7.1), and CCL22 (log2 fold change 7.6), which were the most induced cytokine or chemokine transcripts in poly I:C-treated TOs (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: DOs expressed chemokines at high basal levels, which were not further induced by poly I:C treatment and did not induce any CCL22.
claims.source: In contrast, DOs expressed chemokines at high basal levels, which were not further induced by poly I:C treatment and did not induce any CCL22 (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Transcripts most selectively induced in DOs by poly I:C treatment included CD38 and the phospholipase PLA1A.
claims.source: Transcripts most selectively induced in DOs included CD38 and the phospholipase PLA1A (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The topmost induced factors in poly I:C-treated TOs were the chemokines CCL22, CXCL5, CXCL2, and CX3CL1.
claims.source: The topmost induced factors in poly I:C-treated TOs were the chemokines CCL22, CXCL5, CXCL2, and CX3CL1 (Figure 5D, left), which was consistent with their transcriptional upregulation by RNASeq (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: PCA of Luminex-based profiling of poly I:C treated TOs and DOs revealed organoid-specific responses to this treatment, which included the specific induction of CCL22 in poly I:C treated TOs.
claims.source: PCA of Luminex-based profiling of poly I:C treated TOs and DOs revealed organoid-specific responses to this treatment, which included the specific induction of CCL22 in poly I:C treated TOs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: Type III IFNs IFN-λ1 and IFN-λ2 were induced by both TOs and DOs in response to poly I:C treatment and were the topmost induced factors in DOs.
claims.source: Factors induced by both TOs and DOs included the type III IFNs IFN-λ1 and IFN-λ2 (Figure 5G and H), which were the topmost induced factors in DOs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claims.claim: Type I IFNs IFN-α2 and IFNβ were induced to significantly greater levels in TOs than DOs in response to poly I:C treatment.
claims.source: In contrast, the type I IFNs IFN-α2 and IFNβ were induced to significantly greater levels in TOs than DOs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claims.claim: DOs were highly permissive to HCMV infection as quantified by detectable GFP or mCherry expression of viral gene expression in most organoids.
claims.source: We found that DOs were highly permissive to HCMV infection as quantified by detectable GFP or mCherry expression of viral gene expression in most organoids (Figure 6A, C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6A, C and D.

claims.claim: TOs were largely resistant to HCMV infection, with low levels of infection by AD169r and almost undetectable levels by TB40E.
claims.source: In contrast, TOs were largely resistant to HCMV infection, with low levels of infection by AD169r and almost undetectable levels by TB40E, as assessed by fluorescence of tagged viral gene expression (Figure 6B, C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 6B, C and D.

claims.claim: The HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9 and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs.
claims.source: Consistent with this, analysis of the expression of key HCMV products using bulk RNASeq from infected TOs and DOs showed that the HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9, which is important for HCMV DNA replication (Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020), and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: RNA4.9 is important for HCMV DNA replication.
claims.source: Consistent with this, analysis of the expression of key HCMV products using bulk RNASeq from infected TOs and DOs showed that the HCMV-associated factors RNA4.9, which is important for HCMV DNA replication (Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020), and UL63 were significantly lower in TOs compared to DOs (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Tai-Schmiedel et al., 2020.

claims.claim: There was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection in TOs under EVT differentiation conditions despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs.
claims.source: Despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs under differentiated conditions, we found that there was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection under these conditions (Figure 6F and G), suggesting that EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 6F and G.

claims.claim: EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
claims.source: Despite the significant enrichment of HLA-G positive EVTs under differentiated conditions, we found that there was no significant enhancement of HCMV infection under these conditions (Figure 6F and G), suggesting that EVTs are not the primary targets of HCMV infection in TOs.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EVT differentiation did not enhance HCMV infection.

claims.claim: TOs responded to HCMV infection through the differential expression of 282 transcripts (AD169r strain) or 173 transcripts (TB40E strain), of which ~38% were shared between both strains of HCMV.
claims.source: TOs responded to HCMV infection through the differential expression of 282 transcripts (AD169r strain) or 173 transcripts (TB40E strain), of which ~38% were shared between both strains of HCMV (Figure 7A and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claims.claim: DOs responded to HCMV infection with 95 (AD169r strain) or 117 (TB40E strain) transcripts differentially expressed by this infection.
claims.source: By contrast, DOs responded to HCMV infection less robustly, with 95 (AD169r strain) or 117 (TB40E strain) transcripts differentially expressed by this infection (Figure 7B and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claims.claim: Only 3-4% of differentially expressed transcripts were shared between TOs and DOs infected with AD169r or TB40E.
claims.source: Of these differentially expressed transcripts, only 3–4% were shared between TOs and DOs infected with AD169r (Figure 7E) or TB40E (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 7E and F.

claims.claim: Only three transcripts were induced by both strains of HCMV in both TOs and DOs and included CCNA1 (Cyclin A1), the ISG OAS2, and EPSTI1 (Epithelial Stromal Interaction 1).
claims.source: Of these shared transcripts, only three were induced by both strains of HCMV in both TOs and DOs and included CCNA1 (Cyclin A1), the ISG OAS2, and EPSTI1 (Epithelial Stromal Interaction 1) (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Transcripts specifically induced by HCMV infection of TOs included H3Y1 (H3.Y Histone 1), KHDC1L (KH Domain Containing 1 Like), several members of the PRAME Family (PRAMEF2, 8, 12, 14, and 20), and TRIM49A and B (Tripartite Motif Containing 43).
claims.source: Transcripts specifically induced by HCMV infection of TOs included H3Y1 (H3.Y Histone 1), KHDC1L (KH Domain Containing 1 Like), several members of the PRAME Family (PRAMEF2, 8, 12, 14, and 20), and TRIM49A and B (Tripartite Motif Containing 43) (Figure 7H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7H.

claims.claim: DO-specific transcripts induced by HCMV infection included several components of the nitric oxide signaling pathway including NOS2 (Nitric Oxide Synthase 2), DUOX2 (Dual Oxidase 2), and DUOXA2 (Dual Oxidase Maturation Factor 2) as well as CXCL10 and CSF3/G-CSF.
claims.source: In contrast, DO-specific transcripts included several components of the nitric oxide signaling pathway including NOS2 (Nitric Oxide Synthase 2), DUOX2 (Dual Oxidase 2), and DUOXA2 (Dual Oxidase Maturation Factor 2) as well as CXCL10 and CSF3/G-CSF (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claims.claim: TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), IL-8, and IL-11.
claims.source: We found that TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment (Breviario et al., 1992), IL-8, and IL-11 (Figure 8A, C and D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 8A, C and D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Pentraxin-3 (PTX3) was first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment.
claims.source: We found that TOs secreted relatively few cytokines in response to HCMV infection, including pentraxin-3 (PTX3), first described as an endothelial factor induced by IL-1β treatment (Breviario et al., 1992), IL-8, and IL-11 (Figure 8A, C and D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Breviario et al., 1992.

claims.claim: DOs responded to HCMV infection by secreting both proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., CXCL10, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, and IL-6) and through the release of the type III IFN IFN-λ2.
claims.source: In contrast, DOs responded to HCMV infection by secreting both proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (e.g., CXCL10, MIP-1α, MIP-1β, and IL-6) and through the release of the type III IFN IFN-λ2 (Figure 8B, C and E, Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex-based profiling data shown in Figure 8B, C and E, and Figure 8—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: DOs did not induce any other detectable IFNs such as IFN-α2 or IFN-β or IFN-λ1 in response to HCMV infection.
claims.source: In contrast to IFN-λ2, DOs did not induce any other detectable IFNs such as IFN-α2 or IFN-β or IFN- λ1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C-E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Luminex assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C-E.

claims.claim: Treatment of DOs with ruxolitinib significantly increased levels of HCMV replication.
claims.source: We found that treatment of DOs with ruxolitinib significantly increased levels of HCMV replication, which correlated with higher levels of GFP fluorescence (Figure 8F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8F and G.

claims.claim: Treatment of TOs with ruxolitinib did not increase levels of HCMV replication over DMSO treated controls.
claims.source: In contrast, treatment of TOs with ruxolitinib did not increase levels of HCMV replication over DMSO treated controls, which remained low under both ruxolitinib-treated and DMSO-treated conditions (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: Co-culturing of DOs and TOs led to a significant reduction in HCMV infection in DOs compared to singly cultured DOs.
claims.source: We found that whereas singly cultured DOs were permissive to HCMV infection, co-culturing of DOs and TOs led to a significant reduction in HCMV infection in DOs (Figure 8I and J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative infection data shown in Figure 8I and J.

claims.claim: PHT cells from full-term placentas and mid-gestation chorionic villi constitutively release type III IFNs, which protect trophoblasts from viral infections.
claims.source: We showed previously that PHT cells isolated from full-term placentas and mid-gestation chorionic villi constitutively release type III IFNs, which protect trophoblasts from viral infections (Bayer et al., 2016; Corry et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Bayer et al., 2016 and Corry et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The decidua may be a primary site of replication for several microorganisms associated with congenital disease, including HCMV, ZIKV, and Listeria monocytogenes.
claims.source: The decidua may be a primary site of replication for several microorganisms associated with congenital disease, including HCMV (McDonagh et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2003; Weisblum et al., 2015), ZIKV (Guzeloglu-Kayisli et al., 2020; Platt et al., 2018; Weisblum et al., 2017), and Listeria monocytogenes (Rizzuto et al., 2017), suggesting it may serve as a reservoir for these infections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claims.claim: Human trophoblasts constitutively release antiviral interferons (IFNs) that restrict infection in both autocrine and paracrine manners.
claims.source: For example, human trophoblasts constitutively release antiviral interferons (IFNs) that restrict infection in both autocrine and paracrine manners (Bayer et al., 2016; Corry et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Bayer et al., 2016 and Corry et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Constitutive release of IFNs is a unique feature of trophoblasts as IFNs are tightly regulated in most cell types and induced only after detection of the products of viral replication.
claims.source: Constitutive release of IFNs is a unique feature of trophoblasts as IFNs are tightly regulated in most cell types and induced only after detection of the products of viral replication (reviewed in Lazear et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a review by Lazear et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The risk of transplacental transmission of HCMV infection from mother to fetus is only 20% in the first trimester but can reach up to 75% in the third trimester.
claims.source: For instance, the risk of transplacental transmission of HCMV infection from mother to fetus is only 20% in the first trimester but can reach up to 75% in the third trimester, highlighting the relevance of our organoid model for studying placental HCMV infection across gestation (Pass and Anderson, 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Pass and Anderson, 2014.

claims.claim: CXCL10 was highly upregulated in HCMV-infected DOs, consistent with prior findings of increased CXCL10 secretion in decidua explants infected with HCMV ex vivo.
claims.source: CXCL10 was highly upregulated in HCMV-infected DOs, consistent with prior findings of increased CXCL10 secretion in decidua explants infected with HCMV ex vivo (Weisblum et al., 2017; Weisblum et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Weisblum et al., 2017 and Weisblum et al., 2015.

claims.claim: IL-8 was highly induced in HCMV-infected TOs, mirroring the increased IL-8 secretion that has been observed in response to ex vivo HCMV infection of isolated trophoblasts and placental explants.
claims.source: IL-8 was also highly induced in HCMV-infected TOs, mirroring the increased IL-8 secretion that has been observed in response to ex vivo HCMV infection of isolated trophoblasts (Kovács et al., 2007) and placental explants (Weisblum et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Kovács et al., 2007 and Weisblum et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Type III IFNs control HCMV infection in the maternal decidua.
claims.source: Moreover, our data demonstrate that type III IFNs control HCMV infection in the maternal decidua but suggest that additional factors or pathways beyond IFN signaling may restrict HCMV infection of trophoblasts.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the ruxolitinib treatment experiments showing that inhibiting IFN signaling increases HCMV infection in DOs.

claims.claim: Additional factors or pathways beyond IFN signaling may restrict HCMV infection of trophoblasts.
claims.source: Moreover, our data demonstrate that type III IFNs control HCMV infection in the maternal decidua but suggest that additional factors or pathways beyond IFN signaling may restrict HCMV infection of trophoblasts.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ruxolitinib treatment did not increase HCMV infection in TOs.

claims.claim: Ablation of type III IFN signaling in the murine placenta enhances infection of ZIKV in maternal decidua tissue.
claims.source: Indeed, ablation of type III IFN signaling in the murine placenta enhances infection of ZIKV in maternal decidua tissue (Jagger et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Jagger et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Trophoblast-derived effectors, including IFN-λ, work in paracrine to suppress HCMV infection in cells comprising the maternal decidua.
claims.source: The co-culture model presented here also supports a model in which trophoblast-derived effectors, including IFN-λ, work in paracrine to suppress HCMV infection in cells comprising the maternal decidua.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-culture experiments showing that TOs protect DOs from HCMV infection.

claims.claim: Human trophoblasts and mid-gestation chorionic villi respond to T. gondii infection through the selective release of CCL22.
claims.source: We have shown previously that human PHTs and mid-gestation chorionic villi also respond to T. gondii infection through the selective release of CCL22 (Ander et al., 2018; Rudzki et al., 2021), suggesting that this chemokine may be key mediator of the response of the human placenta to microbial infections.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work by Ander et al., 2018 and Rudzki et al., 2021.

claims.claim: CCL22 induction may directly impact maternal-fetal tolerance in the context of congenital infection.
claims.source: Given that Treg infiltration into the decidua has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including miscarriage (Freier et al., 2015), CCL22 induction may directly impact maternal-fetal tolerance in the context of congenital infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CCL22 is a Treg chemoattractant and Treg infiltration is associated with adverse outcomes.

claims.claim: Treg infiltration into the decidua has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including miscarriage.
claims.source: Given that Treg infiltration into the decidua has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes including miscarriage (Freier et al., 2015), CCL22 induction may directly impact maternal-fetal tolerance in the context of congenital infection.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Freier et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Serum isolated from pregnant women often contains elevated levels of cytokines secreted by trophoblasts, indicating that at least some have reached the systemic circulation.
claims.source: Consistent with this concept, serum isolated from pregnant women often contains elevated levels of these cytokines, indicating that at least some have reached the systemic circulation (Benyo et al., 2001; Liu et al., 2019; Megli et al., 2021; Vassiliadis et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

results.result: Trophoblast organoids (TOs) and decidua organoids (DOs) were successfully generated from mid-to-late gestation (26-41 weeks) human placentas. Despite the known decrease in trophoblast stem/progenitor cells after the first trimester, organoids were isolated from all 15 unique placentas, with Ki67-positive proliferative cells identified in full-term chorionic villi.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence for successful organoid generation from mid-to-late gestation tissue. The presence of Ki67-positive cells (C4) validates the existence of progenitor cells in full-term tissue, supporting the feasibility of organoid generation (C1, C2). The high proliferative capacity (C5) confirms organoid viability. The citation to prior work (C3) appropriately contextualizes the challenge overcome.

results.result: TOs and DOs express distinct tissue-specific markers and secrete characteristic factors. TOs express trophoblast markers (SIGLEC6, SDC-1) and secrete hCG, while DOs express decidual markers (MUC5AC) and secrete MUC16. The apical surface of the syncytiotrophoblast in TOs is inward-facing, consistent with first trimester organoids.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C12 collectively demonstrate that TOs and DOs recapitulate their tissues of origin through multiple complementary markers. Immunofluorescence (C6-C8), functional secretion assays (C10-C12), and 3D structural analysis (C9) provide robust, multi-modal validation. The consistency with prior first trimester organoid models (C9) strengthens the interpretation.

results.result: TOs can be differentiated into an EVT-enriched phenotype, with HLA-G positive cells increasing from ~18% to ~96%, accompanied by elevated MMP-2 secretion consistent with EVT characteristics.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 demonstrate successful EVT differentiation through quantitative immunofluorescence and functional secretion assays. The citation to prior work (C15) validates MMP-2 as an appropriate EVT marker. The dramatic increase in HLA-G positive cells provides strong evidence for differentiation efficiency.

results.result: TOs and DOs exhibit distinct transcriptional profiles. TOs express placental markers (HSD3B1, XAGE2/3, GATA3, ERVW-1, PSGs, CGA) and placenta-specific microRNAs (C19MC family), while DOs express decidual markers (MUC1, MUC5A/B, SOX17, HOXB8). TOs cluster with first trimester placental tissue and express first trimester-associated factors like KISS1.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C26 provide comprehensive transcriptional validation through RNASeq, qPCR, and comparative analyses. The differential expression patterns (C16-C20), tissue-specific microRNA expression (C21-C22), sex-specific gene expression (C23), and clustering with first trimester tissue (C24-C26) collectively demonstrate that organoids recapitulate their tissues of origin. The citations appropriately support prior knowledge claims.

results.result: TOs and DOs exhibit distinct basal immunological secretomes. TOs secrete only IL-6, IFN-λ2, and three soluble receptors, while DOs release 21 immune factors including CXCL1, CXCL5, and IL-8. This recapitulates secretory phenotypes observed in primary cells and tissue explants.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29 demonstrate differential secretomes through comprehensive Luminex profiling and PCA analysis. The consistency with prior work on primary cells and explants (C30-C31) validates the biological relevance of the organoid models. The stark difference in secretome complexity between TOs and DOs is well-documented.

results.result: TOs constitutively secrete type III IFN (IFN-λ2) but not type I IFNs or IFN-λ1, recapitulating the unique phenotype of primary human trophoblasts. DOs do not basally secrete IFNs. TO-derived conditioned media induces ISGs and protects non-placental cells from ZIKV infection. EVT-differentiated TOs show reduced IFN-λ2 secretion, suggesting EVTs are not the primary producers.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C40 and C70-C73 provide comprehensive evidence for constitutive IFN-λ2 secretion from TOs through Luminex assays (C32-C35), functional reporter assays (C36), and antiviral protection experiments (C37-C38). The comparison to primary cells (C34, C70) and the EVT differentiation experiment (C39-C40) strengthen the interpretation. The citations appropriately contextualize this unique trophoblast feature (C72-C73).

results.result: TOs and DOs differentially respond to poly I:C treatment. TOs upregulated 448 transcripts including chemokines (CXCL5, CX3CL1, CCL22) and type I IFNs, while DOs upregulated 121 transcripts including CD38 and PLA1A. Only 69 transcripts (mostly ISGs) were shared. Both organoid types induced type III IFNs (IFN-λ1/λ2), which were the top induced factors in DOs.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C50 demonstrate organoid-specific responses to TLR3 activation through comprehensive RNASeq and Luminex profiling. The differential transcriptional responses (C42-C46), protein secretion patterns (C47-C50), and limited overlap (C43) are well-documented. The consistency between transcriptional and protein data strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: DOs are highly permissive to HCMV infection (both AD169r and TB40E strains), while TOs are largely resistant. HCMV-associated factors (RNA4.9, UL63) are significantly lower in TOs. EVT differentiation does not enhance HCMV infection in TOs, suggesting EVTs are not primary targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 demonstrate differential HCMV susceptibility through fluorescence microscopy (C51-C52), RNASeq (C53-C54), and EVT differentiation experiments (C55-C56). The use of two HCMV strains strengthens the conclusions. The inference that EVTs are not primary targets (C56) is appropriately supported by the differentiation experiment (C55).

results.result: TOs and DOs exhibit distinct transcriptional responses to HCMV infection. TOs differentially expressed 282 (AD169r) or 173 (TB40E) transcripts, while DOs expressed 95 (AD169r) or 117 (TB40E) transcripts. Only 3-4% of transcripts were shared, with only three (CCNA1, OAS2, EPSTI1) induced by both strains in both organoid types. TO-specific transcripts included PRAME family members and TRIM49A/B, while DO-specific transcripts included nitric oxide pathway components (NOS2, DUOX2, DUOXA2) and CXCL10.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 demonstrate organoid-specific transcriptional responses through comprehensive RNASeq analysis. The minimal overlap (C59-C60) and distinct response signatures (C61-C62) are well-documented. The use of two HCMV strains provides robustness to the findings.

results.result: TOs and DOs exhibit distinct cytokine responses to HCMV infection. TOs secreted pentraxin-3, IL-8, and IL-11, while DOs secreted proinflammatory cytokines/chemokines (CXCL10, MIP-1α/β, IL-6) and IFN-λ2 but not other IFNs. These responses recapitulate findings from ex vivo tissue explants and isolated trophoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 and C75-C76 demonstrate differential cytokine responses through Luminex profiling. The consistency with prior ex vivo studies (C75-C76) validates the biological relevance. The citations appropriately support prior knowledge (C64) and contextualize the findings.

results.result: Type III IFNs control HCMV infection in DOs but not TOs. Ruxolitinib (JAK inhibitor) treatment significantly increased HCMV replication in DOs but not in TOs, suggesting additional IFN-independent factors restrict HCMV infection in trophoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 demonstrate differential IFN dependence through pharmacological inhibition experiments. The inferences about IFN control in DOs (C77) and additional restriction factors in TOs (C78) are appropriately supported by the differential ruxolitinib responses. However, the mechanism of TO resistance remains incompletely defined.

results.result: Co-culturing TOs and DOs significantly reduces HCMV infection in DOs compared to singly cultured DOs, demonstrating that trophoblast-derived factors (including IFN-λ) protect decidual cells from HCMV infection in a paracrine manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C80, and C97 demonstrate paracrine protection through a co-culture model. The significant reduction in DO infection when co-cultured with TOs (C69) supports the inference of paracrine protection (C80, C97). However, the specific factors mediating protection beyond IFN-λ are not definitively identified.

These citations support background knowledge, validate marker choices, and position the current work within the existing literature. No obvious misattributions or incorrect citations are apparent.
